papers.title: Hints of self-interacting dark matter from strong gravitational lensing
papers.authors: Daniel Gilman, Kalliopi Petraki, Thomas Pignard, James Gurian, Alex Kusenko, Anna Nierenberg
papers.abstract: An analysis of 29 quadruply imaged quasars hints at dark matter halo densities consistent with gravothermal core collapse, a key prediction of self-interacting dark matter. We interpret this evidence through elastic Yukawa scattering, combining lensing with upper limits on the cross-section strength from galaxy clusters and Milky Way satellite evaporation. Favored models have dark matter masses of $20$-$80\,{\rm GeV}$, MeV-scale mediators, and Yukawa-potential strengths near $10^{-3}$, yielding cross-sections of $10^2$--$10^4 \, {\rm cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ at $10\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$. Cosmological, direct and indirect detection bounds on MeV-scale mediators motivate a neutrinophilic scalar dilepton that decays invisibly without Higgs mixing. These results demonstrate how inferences on core collapse constrain dark sector physics.

The authors map these lensing-inferred density signatures to a particle physics model involving Yukawa scattering, finding that the data favor cross-sections that induce core collapse in low-mass halos. This work demonstrates how small-scale structure observations can constrain dark sector parameters, such as mediator mass and coupling strength, while remaining consistent with existing cluster and satellite galaxy constraints.

The analysis disfavors standard CDM with Bayes factors ranging from 8:1 to 24:1, depending on the assumed subhalo properties and tidal evolution models.
The results are consistent with independent upper limits on self-interaction from galaxy cluster scales and Milky Way satellite evaporation.

papers.title: When precise inference is wrong: Diagnosing model misspecification with applications to cosmic dawn and reionisation
papers.authors: Daniela Breitman
papers.abstract: As observations of the cosmic dawn (CD) and epoch of reionisation (EoR) rapidly improve in precision, the approximate forward models used to interpret them might struggle to keep pace. Bayesian inference with a misspecified model, one that cannot represent the processes generating the observations, can yield tightly constrained, yet misleading and biased astrophysics, with different parts of the observations favouring incompatible parameter values. Model misspecification can evade a $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit test, and Bayesian model selection requires a better model, which is not always available. We therefore apply the suspiciousness, a statistic developed to quantify tensions between datasets, to CD/EoR inference as a model criticism tool that tests whether these parts can be explained by the same parameters. We first apply it to HERA 21-cm power spectrum (PS) upper limits, which are too weak to reveal misspecification, as expected, and to HST and JWST UV luminosity functions (LFs). Under our galaxy model, the UV LFs at $z\leq10$ and $z>10$ are in tension at $5.0\sigma$ in the Gaussian limit, a failure visible in the fits, although doubling the uncertainties of the $z>10$ observations reduces it to $2.1\sigma$. Finally, we analyse a mock SKA-Low AA$^\ast$ 1080 h 21-cm PS with the model that generated it and with a simpler, misspecified model. We find that the misspecified model silently fails: it fits the PS well, passing visual inspection and, for most noise realisations, a $\chi^2$ test, yet its inferred astrophysics is wrong. The Bayesian evidence disfavours it, but only relative to the true model, which is unavailable for real observations. The suspiciousness finds no tension for the well-specified model, but a $\sim3.4\sigma$ tension for the misspecified one, strongly ruling it out without requiring a more adequate candidate model.

To address this without requiring an explicit alternative model, the author adopts 'suspiciousness' (a Bayesian internal consistency metric quantifying tension between dataset subsets) as a model criticism tool. Using the fast 21cmEMU neural-network emulator suite, the diagnostic is applied to real HERA 21-cm upper limits, HST and JWST UV luminosity functions, and mock SKA 21-cm power spectrum detections. The diagnostic successfully uncovers hidden model misspecifications—such as a $3.4\sigma$ internal tension when fitting mock SKA data with an incomplete galaxy model—even when the misspecified model passes visual and standard $\chi^2$ goodness-of-fit checks.

papers.title: Model-independent and reconstruction-free evidence for cosmic acceleration from DESI baryon acoustic oscillations
papers.authors: Laura Herold, Graeme E. Addison, Adam G. Riess
papers.abstract: While there is ample evidence that the universe's expansion is accelerating, most of this evidence relies on assuming a shape of the relative expansion rate, $H(z)/H_0$, informed by a cosmological model or a kinematical approach. Model-independent analyses are common for supernova datasets but rarely applied to other data. In this work, we use uncalibrated baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) from DESI DR2 for a model-independent test of acceleration, which makes no assumptions about the theory of gravity or the energy content of the universe. We test for cosmic acceleration with three model-independent statistics that rely purely on the measured Alcock-Paczyński parameter, the isotropic BAO, and the line-of-sight BAO, and do not require any reconstruction between redshift bins unlike previous analyses. Accounting for the look-elsewhere effect, among all statistics we find $2.4\sigma$ - $4.1\sigma$ evidence for cosmic acceleration within $0 \leq z \leq 0.934$ when assuming flatness; allowing for spatial curvature, $|\Omega_k| \leq 1$, at least two of the three statistics retain $2.4\sigma$ - $3.5\sigma$.

To bypass these assumptions, the authors propose three model-independent, reconstruction-free statistical tests ($S_F$, $S_V$, and $S_{VH}$) built purely from geometric ratios of Alcock-Paczyński parameters and BAO distances ($D_V$ and $D_H$). Applying these tests directly to DESI DR2 BAO measurements across $0 \le z \le 0.934$ without assuming Friedmann equations or dark energy properties, they evaluate the null hypothesis of a non-accelerating universe. This provides a robust, purely geometric confirmation of cosmic acceleration from BAO alone that is entirely independent of gravity theories, dark energy models, or data smoothing techniques.
conclusions: Developed three model-independent, reconstruction-free statistics based on $F_{\rm AP}$, $D_V$, and $D_V/D_H$ to test for cosmic acceleration using uncalibrated BAO data.

Assuming spatial flatness, DESI DR2 BAO data yield $2.4\sigma$ to $4.1\sigma$ evidence for cosmic acceleration within $0 \le z \le 0.934$ after accounting for the look-elsewhere effect, with the hybrid statistic $S_{VH}$ providing the highest significance ($4.1\sigma$ point-wise max, $3.2\sigma$ redshift-averaged).
Allowing for non-zero spatial curvature ($|\Omega_k| \le 1$), at least two of the statistics retain $2.4\sigma$ to $3.5\sigma$ evidence for acceleration.

The analysis confirms cosmic acceleration geometrically from BAO measurements alone without relying on redshift-reconstruction algorithms (e.g., Gaussian processes) that can introduce method-dependent biases.

papers.title: From Quantum Field Fluctuations to High-Redshift AGN: Semiclassical Origins of Halo Mass Function Constraints in the JWST Era
papers.authors: Elan Yogeswaren, Amir-Homayoon Najmi, Robert K Schaefer
papers.abstract:
We develop a continuous framework connecting quantum field fluctuations in the early Universe to the abundance and observable properties of galaxies and active galactic nuclei (AGN) at cosmic dawn. Beginning with quantum fields in curved Friedmann Lemaitre Robertson Walker spacetime, we follow inflationary vacuum fluctuations into the primordial curvature spectrum, linear matter power spectrum, mass variance $\sigma(MHz)$, mass peak height $
u(MHz)$, and the statistics of nonlinear halo formation. The Press-Schechter and Sheth-Tormen formalisms provide an analytic description of halo abundance and its dependence on peak rarity. A complementary high redshift halo mass function calibrated with the GUREFT simulations of Yung et al. (2024) provides a numerical description specifically constructed for the cosmic dawn regime probed by JWST. The comparison between these analytic and simulation calibrated prescriptions provides a direct measure of the sensitivity of predicted halo populations to the observations. We separate this cosmological supply of halos from the astrophysical and observational mappings that produce stars, ultraviolet luminosities, and active galactic nuclei. Controlled numerical experiments show that a percent level perturbation in the primordial fluctuation amplitude produces only a modest change in $\sigma$ and $
u$, but can strongly amplify the exponentially suppressed high $
u$ tail of the Halo Mass Function. This sensitivity increases toward high halo mass and high redshift, identifying rare cosmic dawn populations as potentially powerful probes of primordial statistics while simultaneously exposing the importance of uncertainties in halo abundance. High redshift AGN population statistics and the Ultraviolet Luminosity Function provide additional constraints on the primordial power spectrum and dynamics of primordial inflation theory.

To address this, the authors construct an end-to-end analytical and numerical pipeline tracking perturbations from quantum field fluctuations in FLRW spacetime, through slow-roll inflation and linear density evolution, down to nonlinear halo statistics and observable galaxy UV luminosity functions. They compare the traditional analytic Sheth-Tormen halo mass function against the high-redshift GUREFT simulation-calibrated mass function (Yung et al. 2024) to evaluate how sensitivities propagate along the chain. This diagnostic framework illustrates how uncertainties in nonlinear halo mass function calibrations and galaxy-to-halo mappings can produce observational signatures that are degenerate with modifications to the primordial power spectrum.
conclusions: Develops a continuous end-to-end calculation connecting inflationary quantum field perturbations to high-redshift galaxy UV luminosity functions and supermassive black hole host halo abundances at cosmic dawn ($z > 6$).

Demonstrates that percent-level shifts in the primordial perturbation amplitude $A_s$ generate modest changes in linear peak height $\nu(M,z)$, but become exponentially amplified in the extreme high-mass, high-redshift tail of the halo mass function.

Shows via a direct Sheth-Tormen versus GUREFT simulation calibration comparison that halo mass function uncertainties in the rare-peak regime can mimic or degenerate with alterations in primordial fluctuation statistics.

Argues that JWST high-redshift anomalies should be treated as stress-tests of the entire quantum-to-observation mapping rather than direct evidence for a failure of $\Lambda$CDM or standard single-field inflation.

papers.title: FOMO-Z. Optimal galaxy classification, photometric redshifts, and reconstruction of population distributions
papers.authors: G. F. Lesci
papers.abstract: We present FOMO-Z (Flexible Optimizer of Multi-dimensional Operators and photo-$z$s), a set of statistical methods implemented in Python for galaxy classification and probabilistic inference from photometry. The methods use a reference sample with known galaxy properties. They rely on explicit, physically interpretable criteria and make no assumptions about the functional form of the color distributions. Binary selections are calibrated using either linear color conditions, particularly suited to background galaxy selection, or flexible color--color grids, seeking to maximize completeness given a threshold on purity. For probabilistic inference, the code identifies reference objects with compatible colors within photometric uncertainties to estimate each test galaxy's probability of satisfying user-defined criteria, as well as probability density functions of continuous properties such as redshift. The code also reconstructs property distributions of selected galaxy populations using photometrically similar galaxies in the reference sample. This framework supports prior weights and reference redshift probability distributions. A built-in feature-selection method identifying informative colors is also introduced. We demonstrate applications to background galaxy selection, galaxy population classification, tomographic redshift calibration, and photometric redshift estimation. The code achieves results consistent with those obtained through machine-learning approaches, such as self-organizing maps, while remaining computationally efficient, making it suitable for large photometric surveys and future Stage IV cosmological analyses. The code is publicly available at this https URL .

The code implements both binary classification (calibrating color cuts to maximize completeness at a fixed purity) and probabilistic methods (estimating individual membership probabilities and reconstructing property distributions). This tool is particularly relevant for Stage IV surveys like Euclid, where efficient, interpretable methods are needed to handle large datasets and optimize the trade-off between sample purity and completeness in cosmological analyses.

The code achieves performance comparable to more complex machine-learning approaches (e.g., self-organizing maps) while maintaining high computational efficiency and transparency.

papers.title: Vacuum Phase Transition and Decay to Cross the Phantom Divide
papers.authors: William Giarè, Kushal Lodha, Robert R. Caldwell, Eleonora Di Valentino, Eric V. Linder
papers.abstract: We show that the vacuum metamorphosis model with decay fits current baryon acoustic oscillation and supernova distance data and cosmic microwave background measurements significantly better than $\Lambda$CDM and nearly as well as $w_0w_a$CDM with the same number of parameters. Vacuum metamorphosis with decay provides a physically motivated model of dark energy and an explanation of current cosmological data. In this scenario, non-perturbative quantum effects of a massive scalar field freeze the Ricci scalar curvature when it reaches a critical value proportional to the mass squared, inducing a phase transition in the scalar field, giving a phantom dark energy equation of state $w<-1$. After the phase transition, vacuum energy decays into light particles, providing a natural mechanism for the dark-energy equation of state to cross the phantom divide from $w<-1$ to $w>-1$, in agreement with current cosmological indications, without requiring an explicit coupling to matter.

The authors propose a fundamental physical mechanism for this transition by adding a decay channel to the Vacuum Metamorphosis (VM) model. In this setup, non-perturbative quantum loop corrections freeze the Ricci scalar $R$ at a critical value, inducing a phantom phase, while subsequent exponential decay of the dark energy sector into light particles uplifts $w(z)$ across $w=-1$. Implementing background and linear perturbations in a modified version of CLASS, the authors test the model against DESI DR2, DES-Dovekie SNe Ia, and Planck/ACT/SPT CMB data. The model provides a self-consistent physical explanation for phantom divide crossing without requiring direct dark energy couplings to dark matter.
conclusions: Vacuum Metamorphosis with decay fits current data significantly better than $\Lambda$CDM, with $\Delta\chi^2 = -8.54$ for BAO+CMB+SN and $\Delta\chi^2 = -12.13$ for BAO+CMB.
The model performs comparably to the phenomenological $w_0w_a$CDM parametrization ($\Delta\chi^2 = +5.27$ for BAO+CMB+SN and $-0.25$ for BAO+CMB) while using the same number of extra parameters.
The preferred phase transition redshift occurs at $z_* \sim 1.1 - 1.6$ with a natural dimensionless decay rate $\gamma_* = \Gamma/H(z_*) \approx 1$.
The scalar field decay naturally drives $w(z)$ across $w=-1$ near $z \approx 0.5$, yielding a present-day dark energy equation of state $w_0 \approx -0.8$.

papers.title: The Effect of Large Apertures on Atmospheric Noise Spectra for Millimeter-wave Telescopes
papers.authors: Thomas W. Morris, Neelima Sehgal
papers.abstract: Ground-based millimeter and submillimeter telescopes produce astronomical maps that contain a combination of noise inherent to themselves as well as contamination from foregrounds, with the strongest foreground being fluctuating atmospheric emission. While the emission of the turbulent atmosphere itself follows a scale-free power law, the atmosphere as seen by the telescope is modified by the properties of the instrument optics. A naive power-law extrapolation of the atmospheric noise spectrum ignores the blurring effect of the near-field beam, which becomes more pronounced for larger telescope apertures and at higher multipoles. In this work, we use a toy model to derive a semianalytic estimate of the atmospheric noise spectrum that takes into account the effects of near-field optics. We show that it has an appreciable effect for large-aperture telescopes, suggesting that ultra-sensitive, high-resolution experiments are not necessarily limited by the atmosphere on small angular scales. We also present an estimate of the atmospheric knee as a function of the primary aperture, the atmospheric scale height, and the outer scale of turbulence.

ai.summary: Ground-based millimeter-wave telescopes mapping the cosmic microwave background face significant contamination from atmospheric water vapor turbulence. Standard forecasts typically extrapolate atmospheric noise to high multipoles (small angular scales) using simple power laws, which can overly penalize high-resolution observations. The authors develop a semianalytic model incorporating near-field beam optics, recognizing that for large apertures ($D \gtrsim 8\text{ m}$) the Rayleigh range extends well above the atmospheric scale height, causing the telescope to average over near-field turbulent eddies. They derive closed-form expressions for the map-level atmospheric power spectrum as a function of primary aperture size, field of view, atmospheric scale height, and turbulence correlation length. Their findings indicate that atmospheric noise at high multipoles is suppressed far below conventional power-law expectations, meaning high-resolution ground-based CMB observations are less atmosphere-limited at small scales than previously assumed.
conclusions: Derived a semianalytic 3D model combining near-field beam optics with Kolomogorov atmospheric turbulence theory to predict map-level millimeter-wave noise spectra.

Large primary apertures ($D \gtrsim 8\text{ m}$) suppress small-scale atmospheric noise by orders of magnitude compared to standard power-law extrapolations because the beam footprint averages over turbulent fluctuations near the aperture.
The multipole scale of the atmospheric noise knee is determined by optical design (aperture and field of view) and local atmospheric conditions, rather than survey duration or sky coverage area.
High-resolution, ultra-sensitive ground-based CMB experiments (such as CMB-HD) are unlikely to be fundamentally limited by atmospheric noise at high multipoles.

papers.title: The Dynamical Mass Profiles of Galaxy Groups - Application to IllustrisTNG-300
papers.authors: Alfie Russell, Rita Tojeiro, Anne-Marie Weijmans
papers.abstract: We present a new rescaling and stacking method to test cold dark matter predictions through the dynamical modelling of galaxy groups using the Jeans equation. We test the viability of this method on idealised, line-of-sight group data at $z=0$ in the IllustrisTNG-300 simulation, using subhalos and satellite galaxies as tracers. Dynamical mass profiles are measured using the code `Gravsphere' for seven distinct quality cuts, three on the dark matter substructure and four on the `visible' satellite galaxies. When using the dark matter substructure, we find that selecting subhalos by their infall time onto the group provides the best recovery of the true mass profile. When using satellite galaxies we instead find that selecting quenched satellites provides the best recovery. In both cases the mass profile is recovered within $<1\sigma$ of the true value up to $\sim 1.5$ times the median host virial radius. However, we also find the recovered velocity anisotropy to be biased towards negative values for all seven of our subhalo samples beyond the median host virial radius. This suggests dynamical systematics may still be present in the data, which will need to be quantified in future work before application to surveys.

To overcome this limitation, the authors introduce a concentration-based rescaling and stacking pipeline that combines line-of-sight tracer kinematics across thousands of simulated groups in the IllustrisTNG-300 hydrodynamical simulation. Using higher-order Jeans modeling with the `gravsphere` code, they evaluate how tracer selection cuts—such as subhalo infall time, group relaxation state, or satellite quenching—impact the recovered dynamical mass profiles. They show that selecting quenched satellite galaxies allows accurate recovery of the true enclosed mass profile within $1\sigma$ out to $1.5$ times the median virial radius, providing a viable strategy for application to wide-area spectroscopic surveys like DESI BGS.
conclusions: A halo-concentration rescaling method allows successful stacking of groups across a wide mass range ($10^{11.3} - 10^{14} M_\odot/h$), mapping individual mass profiles onto a single self-similar curve.
Selecting quenched satellite galaxies as tracers provides the best dynamical mass profile recovery, matching the true profile within $1\sigma$ out to $\sim 1.5 r_{200}$.
For dark matter substructures, selecting subhalos that accreted $\gtrsim 4.3\text{ Gyr}$ ago yields unbiased mass profile recovery out to $\sim 2.5 r_{200}$.

Reconstructed velocity anisotropies $\beta(r)$ are systematically biased towards negative (tangential) values beyond $r_{200}$ across all tracer samples, pointing to residual dynamical non-equilibrium or uncleaned line-of-sight interlopers.

papers.title: Primordial black holes and gravitational waves from aligned axion inflation
papers.authors: Nadir Ijaz
papers.abstract: We study the production of primordial black holes (PBHs) and scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs) in aligned axion inflation through the transition between two stages of inflation. The first stage proceeds along a metastable trajectory and ends when this trajectory loses stability, causing the fields to turn towards the attractor of the second inflationary stage. During the transition, coupled adiabatic--entropy evolution produces a localized enhancement of the curvature power spectrum. We compute the PBH abundance from this spectrum assuming Gaussian primordial curvature perturbations and using the nonlinear compaction-function formalism with a spectrum-dependent collapse threshold and critical collapse. Representative benchmark solutions yield asteroid-mass PBHs with a potentially significant dark-matter abundance, together with an associated SIGW background.

papers.title: Two-loop matter power spectrum from FFTLog and kite integrals
papers.authors: Paola Cappellazzi, Johannes M. Henn, Marko Simonović
papers.abstract: We present a fast and accurate method for computing the two-loop matter power spectrum in the Effective Field Theory of Large-Scale Structure (EFTofLSS). Using FFTLog, we decompose the linear power spectrum into complex power laws, reducing the two-loop corrections to cosmology-independent massless Feynman integrals of kite topology. A central numerical challenge is the evaluation of these integrals for complex powers with large imaginary parts, where the highly oscillatory integrands make accurate numerical evaluation particularly challenging. We overcome this difficulty using a Mellin--Barnes representation summed over a uniform lattice, achieving approximately ten digit precision even for large imaginary powers, with an error estimate for each integral. The resulting precomputed matrices allow the two-loop power spectrum to be evaluated for a new cosmology in a few milliseconds. Comparing with direct numerical integration, we find agreement at the $10^{-4}$ level relative to the power spectrum up to $k=0.2$ $h$Mpc$^{-1}$ after accounting for EFTofLSS counterterm contributions and FFTLog decomposition errors. The same framework extends to biased tracers and redshift-space distortions, providing the building blocks for general two-loop calculations in EFTofLSS. We make the code for evaluating the kite integrals publicly available, together with precomputed matrices and an implementation for the two-loop matter power spectrum as a concrete application. Our results can be directly incorporated into existing FFTLog-based codes for large-scale structure, extending their current one-loop capabilities to two loops within the same computational framework.

papers.title: Cosmology with post-EoR 21 cm Intensity Mapping surveys: power spectrum measurements in the last decade
papers.authors: Réza Ansari, Xuelei Chen, Albert Stebbins, Peter Timbie
papers.abstract: The technique of 21 cm intensity mapping (IM) is emerging as a possible, cost-effective method to supplement optical surveys to map the large-scale structure, and extend their redshift reach, with projects aiming to cover a large range of post-EoR redshifts, from z=0 to z=6. Since the early discussions 20 years ago, a few dedicated interferometers have been built, and surveys have been carried out using them as well as general purpose radio instruments. An introduction to late-time cosmology with 21 cm intensity mapping is given, highlighting the main scientific and technical challenges. We present then an overview of different instrument concepts and survey strategies, followed by a discussion of outstanding data analysis challenges, most notably the foreground subtraction, which is a major issue in IM. We carry on with a presentation of the currently active projects and the 21 cm signal measurements which have been obtained, either in cross-correlation with optical surveys, or as the autocorrelation power spectrum. Finally, we discuss briefly the prospects for this field with future instruments and surveys such as SKA, HIRAX and CHORD.

The authors detail the technical challenges of this approach, specifically the difficulty of separating the weak cosmological signal from overwhelming Galactic foregrounds, and discuss the current state of observational progress, including recent cross-correlation and autocorrelation detections. The review concludes by evaluating the prospects for next-generation radio arrays like HIRAX and CHORD to overcome current systematic limitations.

papers.title: Elastic boundaries in Stochastic Inflation
papers.authors: Baptiste Blachier
papers.abstract: In the context of stochastic inflation, specifying boundary conditions is often a requirement to distinguish domains where quantum diffusion takes place from regions where stochastic effects are suppressed compared to the standard slow-roll evolution. Yet, even though the transition between the two is expected to be smooth and continuous, most of the literature has hitherto focused on absorbing and reflective boundaries. We consider here the use of a broader class of boundaries, called elastic, which involves one free parameter interpolating between these two limiting cases. We show how the conventional stochastic-$\delta N$, and its recently proposed time-reversed counterpart adapt to such a class of boundary behaviour. papers.title: Leaking Sound Waves: Gravitational Waves From Dark Sectors Weakly Coupled to the Standard Model

papers.abstract: First-order phase transitions in a dark sector can produce an observable stochastic gravitational-wave background, and many models predicting such signals in current and future experiments have been explored. Within this framework, we analytically show that, even if the bubble expansion initially affects only the dark fluid, sound waves can subsequently be induced in the visible sector. Using the sound-shell model, we find that, despite the additional sound waves generated in the visible sector, the total gravitational-wave signal sourced by both fluids is generally suppressed compared to the case of a completely decoupled dark sector. This suppression becomes more pronounced for larger interaction rates and a larger ratio of relativistic degrees of freedom in the visible sector to those in the dark sector. The coupling also modifies the shape of the gravitational-wave spectrum.

papers.abstract: Joint analyses of high-resolution CMB temperature maps with galaxy surveys provide a unique way to reconstruct the radial velocity field of the underlying matter distribution via the kinematic Sunyaev-Zeldovich (kSZ) effect. Using data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope (ACT) DR6 and the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) DR2, we present radial velocity reconstructions for luminous red galaxies (LRGs), emission-line galaxies (ELGs), and quasars (QSOs). Leveraging the spectroscopic data, we are able to reliably model the foreground contamination and report a negligible impact on our main observables. We detect the velocity-galaxy cross-correlation at $17.0\sigma$ for LRGs, and for the first time, at $8.3\sigma$ for ELGs and $6.8\sigma$ for QSOs. We further report the first detection of the velocity-velocity correlation using LRGs at $3.1\sigma$, as well as the highest cumulative detection of the kSZ effect to date at $20.8 \sigma$. Similarly to previous results, we find a lower amplitude of the kSZ signal compared to our fiducial halo model prediction and electron profile assuming a Battaglia profile. Combining these new observables, we obtain constraints on local-type primordial non-Gaussianity (PNG): $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc} = 15.9_{-34.4}^{+34.6}$ at 68\% confidence, which represents the tightest constraint to date derived from the velocity field. The measurements presented here already exhibit lower noise on a per-mode basis than the galaxy auto-correlation on the largest scales, $k<0.004~\rm{Mpc^{-1}}$, highlighting the key role these observables will play in the context of future CMB experiments such as the Simons Observatory.

papers.title: The Status of Single Scalar Field Dark Energy
papers.authors: Carlos García-García, Pedro G. Ferreira, William J. Wolf
papers.abstract: We present an assessment of the current observational status of single scalar field models of dark energy. Motivated by recent cosmological measurements -- including baryon acoustic oscillations, Type Ia supernovae, and CMB data -- we examine whether a dynamical scalar field offers a viable explanation for the accelerated expansion of the Universe. Working within an effective field theory (EFT) framework, we argue that cosmological observations are fundamentally limited and can at most constrain a small number of parameters that govern scalar field dynamics. We show that quintessence remains only marginally distinguishable from a cosmological constant, $\Lambda$, and that more general EFT extensions exhibit modest statistical preference, though such evidence is sensitive to data set selection and prior assumptions. These extended models generically predict fifth forces and modifications to the growth of structure, raising challenges from astrophysical constraints. We compare their predictions with current growth rate measurements, Integrated Sachs-Wolfe (ISW) effect and Solar System constraints. We emphasize that viable screening mechanisms remain theoretically non-trivial and observationally testable. On the other hand, we find that current ISW and growth data remain largely in agreement. Looking ahead to Stage IV surveys we forecast improvements in constraints on the dark energy behaviour; although there will be some tightening of bounds, we argue that the problem of underdetermination will persist. We conclude that while single scalar field dark energy remains a natural and flexible framework, its ultimate viability will hinge on improved low-redshift growth measurements and a clearer understanding of gravitational screening.

papers.title: Lambda as a Probe of Lensing Consistency
papers.authors: Li Cui, Yuan Shi, Carlo Giocoli
papers.abstract: We introduce a framework to identify the radial transition in mass reconstruction reliability between strong and weak gravitational lensing in galaxy clusters. In weak lensing reconstruction, the convergence recovered from the reduced shear is subject to the mass-sheet degeneracy. We demonstrate that the degeneracy itself can serve as an indicator of the reconstruction reliability, and introduce a spatially resolved parameter $\lambda(r)$ to characterize this as a function of radius. We validate this approach on simulated clusters with realistic observational noise, and show that the radial behavior of $\lambda(r)$ captures the relative reliability of the two probes. Furthermore, when the global mass-sheet parameter $\lambda$ is constrained directly using strong lensing information, the tightest constraints arise where the two probes achieve comparable precision. This provides a quantitative basis for joint strong and weak lensing mass reconstruction.

papers.title: Prospects for Direct Detection of Ultralight Dark Matter candidates in deci-Hz Band with IndIGO-D
papers.authors: Md. Emanuel Hoque, Andrew L. Miller, Arunava Mukherjee
papers.abstract: We investigate the sensitivity of IndIGO-D, a proposed space-based decihertz gravitational-wave interferometer, to different classes of ultralight dark matter. IndIGO-D will probe the $\sim0.01$--$10~\mathrm{Hz}$ frequency band between those accessible to current ground- and future space-based gravitational-wave interferometers, providing access to ultralight dark-matter masses beyond the reach of existing instruments. We consider two complementary signatures: interferometric displacements induced by coherently oscillating scalar (dilaton), vector (dark-photon, $U(1)_B$ and $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge groups), and tensor fields with masses $m_{\rm DM}\sim10^{-17}$--$10^{-14}~\mathrm{eV}$; and changes in laser polarization induced by pseudoscalar axion dark matter at higher masses, around $m_a\sim10^{-12}~\mathrm{eV}$. For the dilatons, dark photons and tensors, we compute the expected sensitivities using two pipelines -- cross-correlation and BSD excess-power -- assuming L-shaped and triangular interferometer layouts and three representative noise power spectral densities (S1, S2, S3), each for two years of continuous observation. We find that the projected sensitivities agree to within a factor of order unity across the search pipelines and interferometer geometries. In particular, we show that IndIGO-D could open previously unconstrained coupling parameter space for vector and tensor dark matter across $m_{\rm DM}\sim10^{-16}$--$10^{-14}~\mathrm{eV}$, bridging the sensitivity of space- and ground-based experiments. For axion dark matter, we demonstrate that a complementary detection for laser light polarization shifts, limited primarily by photon shot noise, could probe the axion-photon coupling $g_{a\gamma}$ at masses around $m_a\sim10^{-12}~\mathrm{eV}$ at a level potentially better than that of other future experiments without degrading sensitivity to gravitational waves.

papers.title: Running cosmological constant in light of recent CMB-BAO data
papers.authors: A. Racioppi, M. Vijar
papers.abstract: We revisit single-field slow-roll inflation driven by a running cosmological constant, i.e. a cosmological constant receiving a logarithmic radiative correction, in light of the latest CMB-BAO data. The relative radiative correction $\delta$ is treated as a free parameter of the model and allowed to be positive or negative. For positive $\delta$, the predictions interpolate between a logarithmic regime and a linear inflation one. Compatibility with CMB-only data is confined to a narrow stripe near the $2\sigma$ border where $\delta$ is relatively large. On the other hand, the predictions fit easily within the constraints including BAO data in a wide range of parameters. For negative $\delta$, the slow-roll approximation breaks down at small field values and the predictions are excluded by data. However, once the effective mass contribution inside the logarithmic correction is taken into account, the negative $\delta$ potential develops a local maximum and behaves like a hilltop model, achieving compatibility with CMB-only data, while agreement with CMB-BAO data is possible only at $2\sigma$.

papers.title: Sterile neutrino dark matter in conformal Majoron models
papers.authors: João Gonçalves, Danny Marfatia, António P. Morais, Vinícius Oliveira, Roman Pasechnik
papers.abstract: We study sterile neutrino dark matter (DM) in a classically conformal U(1)' extension of the Standard Model with three right-handed neutrinos and a Majoron-like singlet scalar that generate the observed pattern of active neutrino masses and mixing via the type-I seesaw mechanism. Working in the regime of strongly suppressed active-sterile mixing, we show that the observed DM abundance can be produced through freeze-in from feeble interactions mediated by the heavy Z' and the conformal scalar. We solve the Boltzmann equation for the nonthermal phase-space distribution and confront the scenario with Lyman-$\alpha$ and strong gravitational lensing data by computing the matter power spectrum. For keV-mass sterile neutrinos we identify the viable parameter space consistent with the inferred relic density and structure-formation and X-ray bounds, including regions compatible with a tentative 3.5 keV line. If a second sterile state is long-lived, late decays can realize a two-component setup that alleviates the $S_8$ tension. However, explanations of the 3.5 keV line and the $S_8$ tension are incompatible with the strong-lensing limit from JWST if the neutrinos saturate the relic abundance. In a highly fine-tuned variant of the model, the 220 PeV KM3NeT event can also be explained by invoking the decay of a superheavy sterile neutrino.

papers.title: VINTERGATAN-GM: long-lived satellite planes induced by a massive GSE-like merger
papers.authors: R. Rodríguez-Cardoso, S. Roca-Fàbrega, Oscar Agertz, Jesus Gallego, Justin Read, Andrew Pontzen, Martin P. Rey, I. Santos-Santos, M. Gámez-Marín, Jess Kocher
papers.abstract: Satellite galaxies in the Local Group tend to be distributed in thin, planar configurations, with many sharing coherent orbital motion. Galaxy formation simulations in $\Lambda$CDM have historically struggled to produce similar structures, leading to the so-called "planes of satellites problem". In this work, we investigate whether the emergence of such structures is connected to the mass of a major merger at $z\sim2$, analogous to the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) event in the Milky Way. We use the VINTERGATAN-GM suite of high-resolution zoom-in simulations, comprising five realizations of the same Milky Way-mass halo generated through targeted genetic modifications of a GSE progenitor. The GSE-like merger mass ratio is systematically varied from 1:10 to 1:2.1, while keeping the final dynamical mass and large-scale environment fixed. We find a clear and consistent trend: more massive GSE-like mergers lead to satellite populations that are both more planar and more kinematically coherent. In particular, simulations with merger mass ratios larger than 1:6 develop Kinematic Persistent Planes (KPPs), in which at least 40% of satellites co-orbit around a common axis over extended periods, comparable to those observed in the Milky Way. These structures arise when sufficiently massive mergers, accreted along the direction of maximum compression of the Lagrangian volume, produce flattened host halos with anisotropic velocity dispersions aligned with the merger direction. The merger aligns the host halo's minor axis with the direction of flattening of the surrounding cosmic web, and planes of satellites then emerge through two complementary processes: (i) satellites preferentially infall along the host's equatorial plane, and (ii) anisotropic dynamical friction in the non-spherical halo gradually reshapes their orbits toward this plane, generating coherent and long-lived planar configurations.

papers.title: Early- and late-time constraints on Wald-Gauss-Bonnet topological dark energy and implications for the $H_0$ and $S_8$ tensions
papers.authors: Stylianos A. Tsilioukas, Fotios K. Anagnostopoulos, Spyros Basilakos, Andronikos Paliathanasis, Emmanuel N. Saridakis
papers.abstract: The persistent $H_0$ and $S_8$ tensions motivate the search for new dark-energy mechanisms capable of modifying the late-time expansion history while preserving the successful early-Universe predictions of $\Lambda$CDM scenario. Wald-Gauss-Bonnet (WGB) topological dark energy provides a physically motivated realization of this possibility, where the effective dark-energy sector emerges from cosmic horizon thermodynamics and the black-hole formation and merger history. We present the first early- and late-Universe analysis of WGB cosmology, implementing the model as an effective fluid in a modified \texttt{CLASS} solver and constraining it against CMB data from \textit{Planck}, ACT~DR6 and SPT-3G, DESI~DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ supernovae. While late-time data alone are consistent with $\Lambda$CDM, the full dataset prefers a non-zero WGB contribution, $\Cn=0.387^{+0.118}_{-0.072}$, corresponding to a $>3\sigma$ phantom-like deviation and an improved fit ($\Delta\chi^2=-10.3$). The preferred solution raises $H_0$ from $68.5$ to $69.8~\kmsmpc$, reducing the Hubble tension by $\sim1\sigma$, at the cost of a mild increase in $S_8$. The reconstructed cosmological observables show that WGB leaves the primary CMB almost unchanged while enhancing lensing and small-scale clustering, revealing a characteristic $H_0$-$S_8$ trade-off. WGB dark energy therefore emerges as a physically motivated and observationally viable late-time mechanism for partially alleviating the Hubble tension without introducing new early-Universe physics.

papers.title: Optimizing the extraction of information from redshift probability distribution functions
papers.authors: Rodrigo Duarte, Valerio Marra
papers.abstract: Photometric redshifts are essential for large-scale structure analyses, yet extracting optimal point estimates and reliability measures from the probability distribution functions (PDZs) delivered by modern photo-$z$ pipelines remains challenging. We introduce turboPDZ, a machine-learning framework using PDZ features and associated observables to optimize redshift point estimates and derive a data-driven reliability score. We apply it to the three independent HSC-SSP PDR3 pipelines (DEmP, DNNz, Mizuki) across Wide and Deep/UltraDeep layers. Each PDZ is compressed via PCA and combined with summary descriptors. A multilayer perceptron, optimized with Optuna under a composite objective ($\sigma_{\rm NMAD}$ and $\eta_{0.15}$), predicts $z_{\rm ml}$. A second network, trained in log-space with MAE and calibrated post hoc, yields an empirical error scale $\sigma_{\rm ml}$, from which the reliability score $r_{\rm ml}$ is derived via percentile ranking. Relative to catalog point estimates, $z_{\rm ml}$ improves both metrics in all six pipeline-layer combinations. Absolute median bias is smaller in four configurations and tied in two. The reliability score achieves the lowest retained-fraction AUC in 10 of 12 native pipeline-layer/metric comparisons. For the Mizuki template-fitting pipeline, catalog reliability indicators have AUC values up to about 13 times larger than those of $r_{\rm ml}$. Feature importance shows that point estimation is dominated by PCA and location statistics, whereas reliability estimation gives greatest weight to peak, PCA, and shape information. The framework is survey-agnostic, but each PDZ dataset requires its own fitted preprocessing, PCA basis, and trained models.
